shortQuestions: Coercive force is the reverse magnetising field needed to reduce the magnetisation of a material to zero.
Steel is a hard magnetic material: carbon atoms and lattice defects pin the domain walls, so the domains are difficult to rotate back. It has a wide hysteresis loop and a large coercive force.
Soft iron is pure and its domains turn easily, so its coercive force is small. This is why steel is used for permanent magnets and soft iron for electromagnets.
Strength is the maximum stress a material can bear before breaking (ultimate tensile strength); stiffness is its resistance to deformation, measured by Young's modulus.

In design both are needed: the structure must not break under the largest expected load (strength, with a safety factor), and it must not bend, sag or vibrate excessively under working loads (stiffness).
For example, bridge girders and building beams use steel, which is both strong and stiff; a material that is strong but not stiff (rubber) or stiff but brittle (glass) is unsuitable for such members.
Superconductivity is the complete loss of electrical resistance of a material below its critical temperature T_c.
Graph of resistance against temperature: as the temperature falls, R decreases gradually, then at T_c it drops suddenly to zero and stays zero.
Example: mercury becomes superconducting at 4.2 K; some ceramic (copper-oxide) materials at about 125 K. A current set up in a superconducting ring flows indefinitely without loss.
Crystalline solids: atoms or ions are arranged in a regular, repeating three-dimensional pattern (long-range order); they have sharp melting points and definite shapes, e.g. NaCl, metals, quartz.
Amorphous solids: no long-range order (only short-range order), like a frozen liquid; they soften over a range of temperature, e.g. glass, pitch.
Polymeric solids: made of very long chain molecules formed by repeated monomer units, partly crystalline and partly amorphous; light and flexible, e.g. polythene, nylon, rubber.
Elastic deformation: the solid regains its original shape and size when the deforming force is removed; it occurs below the elastic limit and obeys Hooke's law.
Plastic deformation: beyond the elastic limit (yield point) the solid is permanently deformed and does not return to its original shape when the force is removed.
Paramagnetic: atoms have permanent magnetic moments that are randomly oriented; weakly attracted by a magnet and slightly magnetised along the field; e.g. aluminium, platinum, oxygen.
Diamagnetic: atoms have no net permanent moment; an external field induces a weak opposite moment, so they are weakly repelled; e.g. copper, bismuth, water.
Ferromagnetic: permanent moments align strongly in domains; strongly attracted, can be magnetised strongly and may retain magnetism; e.g. iron, nickel, cobalt.

Soft magnetic substances (e.g. soft iron) have a narrow, tall hysteresis loop: low coercivity and low retentivity, so they magnetise and demagnetise easily with little energy loss — used for transformer cores and electromagnets.
Hard magnetic substances (e.g. steel, alnico) have a wide hysteresis loop: high coercivity and retentivity, so they keep their magnetism — used for permanent magnets.
(Curves: B against H; the soft-iron loop encloses a small area, the steel loop a large area.)
Brittle materials break suddenly just after the elastic limit, with little or no plastic deformation, e.g. glass, cast iron, ceramics.
Ductile materials undergo large plastic deformation before breaking and can be drawn into wires, e.g. copper, gold, aluminium.
By doping: adding a small amount of a pentavalent impurity (P, As) gives extra free electrons (n-type) and a trivalent impurity (B, Ga) gives holes (p-type).
By raising the temperature or shining light on it, which breaks more covalent bonds and creates more electron–hole pairs.

An MRI machine needs a very strong, steady and uniform magnetic field (about 1.5–3 T), which requires very large currents in its coils.
Superconducting coils have zero resistance, so these large currents flow with no I²R heating and no power loss; once started, the current persists and the field stays very stable.
Ordinary copper coils would need enormous power and cooling to produce such fields.
longQuestions: A tensile force stretches a body (pulls its ends apart), producing tensile stress and an increase in length; a compressive force squeezes it, producing compressive stress and a decrease in length.
In a structure (bridge, truss, building) members carry either tension (ties, cables) or compression (columns, struts); in a loaded beam the top is in compression and the bottom in tension.
For equilibrium the resultant force and resultant torque on every member and joint must be zero: the internal tensile and compressive forces balance the external loads.

Materials are chosen accordingly: steel is strong in tension, concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension (hence reinforced concrete). If a member's stress exceeds its strength it fails and equilibrium is lost.
The stress–strain graph of a ductile metal (e.g. copper) is drawn with strain on the x-axis and stress on the y-axis.
OA: straight line — stress ∝ strain (Hooke's law), A is the proportional limit. Up to B (elastic limit) the wire returns to its original length: this is the elastic region.
Beyond B the material yields: at the yield point (yield stress) the strain increases with little increase in stress — plastic flow region; the deformation is permanent.
Stress then rises to a maximum at C: the ultimate tensile stress (strength). After C the wire narrows (necks) and breaks at the breaking point D.
Young's modulus is the gradient of the linear part OA.
In a solid, the energy levels of the many atoms merge into energy bands.
Valence band: the band occupied by the valence electrons; at 0 K it is completely filled.
Conduction band: the next higher band; electrons in it are free to move and conduct electricity.
Forbidden energy gap E_g: the gap between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band, in which no electron states exist.

Conductors: the bands overlap (E_g = 0). Insulators: large gap (> 3 eV, e.g. diamond ≈ 6 eV). Semiconductors: small gap (Si ≈ 1.1 eV, Ge ≈ 0.7 eV), so some electrons cross it at room temperature, leaving holes in the valence band.
Superconductivity is the state in which a material has zero electrical resistance below a critical temperature T_c (discovered by Kamerlingh Onnes in mercury, T_c = 4.2 K).
Curve: plotting resistance against temperature, R falls steadily on cooling and then drops abruptly to zero at T_c.
A superconductor also expels magnetic field from its interior (Meissner effect) and loses superconductivity in a strong enough magnetic field.
High-temperature superconductors (copper-oxide ceramics) have T_c above 77 K, so they can be cooled with liquid nitrogen.
Uses: MRI magnets, maglev trains, loss-free power cables, particle-accelerator magnets, SQUIDs.
Mechanical properties describe how a solid responds to forces.
Elasticity: the ability to regain shape after deformation. Plasticity: permanent deformation beyond the elastic limit.
Stress = F/A, strain = ΔL/L; their ratio within the elastic limit is the modulus of elasticity: Young's modulus Y (length), bulk modulus K (volume), shear modulus G (shape).
Strength (ultimate tensile stress), stiffness (Young's modulus), ductility (drawn into wires), brittleness (breaks without plastic deformation), hardness and toughness.
These properties are found from the stress–strain graph and decide the use of a material in engineering.
When a ferromagnetic material is taken through a cycle of magnetisation, B is plotted against the magnetising field H (or current).
Starting from zero, B rises along a curve to saturation. When H is reduced to zero, B does not return to zero: the remaining B is the remanence (retentivity).
A reverse field H_c (coercive force) is needed to bring B to zero; further increase gives saturation in the opposite direction, and the cycle completes a closed loop.
This lag of B behind H is hysteresis. The area of the loop equals the energy lost as heat per unit volume per cycle.
For soft iron the loop is narrow (small remanence and coercivity, small loss) — ideal for transformer cores; steel gives a wide loop.
When a wire is stretched by a force, work is done on it and stored as elastic potential (strain) energy.
Within the elastic limit the force increases uniformly from 0 to F as the extension goes from 0 to ΔL; the force–extension graph is a straight line.
Work done = area under the graph = ½ F ΔL. So strain energy U = ½ F ΔL.
Dividing by volume AL: energy per unit volume = ½ (F/A)(ΔL/L) = ½ × stress × strain = ½ Y (strain)².
If the wire is stretched beyond the elastic limit, part of the work is lost as heat and the area under the loading curve is not all recovered.
